title: Tension-Type headache
purpose: Recognise tension-type headache (a primary headache) with the ICHD-3 diagnostic criteria.
structure: Primary headache; mean 1-year prevalence 48.6% worldwide, women and men equally, age 20-40. Subtypes: infrequent episodic, frequent episodic, chronic (frequency and duration differ by subtype).
procedure: History: check that at least 2 of 4 characteristics apply (bilateral; pressing or tightening, not pulsating; mild to moderate intensity, ADLs still possible; not aggravated by routine physical activity such as walking or stairs) and that there is no nausea or vomiting and no more than one of photophobia or phonophobia. Use the HIT-6 questionnaire for impact and a headache diary for duration, intensity and characteristics; headache disorders can overlap.
positive: Criteria fulfilled = tension-type headache; subtype by frequency/duration table.

accuracy.source: n/a (diagnostic criteria page; reference Olesen 2018, ICHD-3)

notes: Not a physical test: the video explains the criteria. ⚠ The frequency/duration table for the three subtypes is an image not present in the API text. ⚠ This page's introduction lists 'medication overdose headaches' among primary headaches, whereas the other headache pages (and the MOH page itself) classify medication overuse headache as secondary. Source writes the prevalence as '48,6%'. More than 60% of primary neck pain patients report concordant headache episodes.

title: Migraine
purpose: Recognise migraine without and with aura (primary headache) with the ICHD-3 criteria.
structure: Primary headache; mean 1-year prevalence 11.2% worldwide, women more than men, age 20-50.
procedure: Without aura: A at least 5 attacks; B attacks last 4-72 h (untreated or unsuccessfully treated); C at least 2 of 4 (unilateral; pulsating; moderate or severe; aggravated by or causing avoidance of routine activity); D during headache nausea and/or vomiting, or photophobia and phonophobia; E not better accounted for by another ICHD-3 diagnosis. With aura: the above plus one or more fully reversible aura symptoms (visual, sensory, speech, motor, brainstem, retinal) and at least 2 of 4: a symptom spreads gradually over 5 min or more and/or symptoms occur in succession; each symptom lasts 5-60 min; at least one symptom is unilateral; headache accompanies or follows within 60 min.
positive: Criteria fulfilled = migraine without or with aura. Aura builds up over 5 minutes, unlike stroke symptoms which appear within seconds.

accuracy.source: n/a (diagnostic criteria page; reference Olesen 2018, ICHD-3)

notes: Not a physical test. The page says 'A-D need to be fulfilled' but then lists criterion E as well. HIT-6 and a headache diary are suggested for impact and characteristics.

title: Cluster Headache
purpose: Recognise cluster headache (primary headache) with the ICHD-3 criteria.
structure: Primary headache; 1-year prevalence 53 per 100,000, men 3-4 times more often than women, age 20-40.
procedure: A at least 5 attacks fulfilling B-D; B untreated episode of 15-180 min with severe or very severe unilateral orbital, supraorbital and/or temporal pain; C at least one ipsilateral sign (conjunctival injection and/or lacrimation; nasal congestion and/or rhinorrhoea; eyelid oedema; forehead and facial sweating; miosis and/or ptosis) and/or restlessness or agitation; D frequency between one every other day and 8 per day; E not better accounted for by another ICHD-3 diagnosis.

accuracy.source: n/a (diagnostic criteria page; reference Olesen 2018, ICHD-3)

notes: Not a physical test. HIT-6 and a headache diary are suggested. The Watson test page is linked as a provocation test for tension-type headache and migraine.

title: Cervicogenic Headache
purpose: Recognise cervicogenic headache (a secondary headache caused by a cervical disorder) with the ICHD-3 criteria.
structure: Secondary headache from bony, disc or soft-tissue elements of the cervical spine (e.g. facet joints, muscles); prevalence 0.7-4%; usually but not always with neck pain.
procedure: Clinical, laboratory and/or imaging evidence of a cervical disorder or lesion known to cause headache, plus at least 2 of: headache developed after onset of the cervical disorder (often a trauma in the history); headache improves or resolves in parallel with the cervical disorder; cervical ROM reduced, pain movement/posture dependent, headache significantly worse on provocative testing (e.g. reduced upper cervical rotation on the flexion-rotation test); headache abolished after diagnostic blockade of a cervical structure or its nerve supply.

accuracy.source: n/a (diagnostic criteria page; reference Olesen 2018, ICHD-3)

notes: Not a physical test. Companion tests: flexion-rotation test (cervical region), Watson headache test, cervicogenic headache explained (mechanism). HIT-6 and a headache diary suggested.

title: Medication Overuse Headache
purpose: Recognise medication overuse headache (secondary headache) with its diagnostic criteria.
structure: Secondary headache; prevalence 1-2% of the general population, women 3-4 times more often, peak around age 40.
procedure: Criteria: headache on 15 or more days per month in a patient with a pre-existing headache disorder; regular overuse for more than 3 months of one or more acute/symptomatic headache drugs (simple analgesics such as paracetamol or NSAIDs on 15 or more days per month; triptans and similar on 10 or more days per month); not better accounted for by another headache disorder. Also ask about excessive caffeine.

accuracy.source: n/a (diagnostic criteria page; reference Kristoffersen & Lundqvist 2014)

notes: Not a physical test. HIT-6 and a headache diary suggested; headache disorders can overlap.

title: Cervicogenic Headache Explained
purpose: Explain the neurophysiology of cervicogenic headache as referred pain (convergence-projection theory).
structure: Deep upper cervical structures with low nociceptive innervation density (C2/3 facet joints and capsules, alar ligaments) converge on second-order neurons in the dorsal horn at C1/C2, the same segment where the ophthalmic branch of the trigeminal nerve converges (pars caudalis of the trigeminal nucleus).
procedure: Explanation page: nociception from the neck reaches the C1/C2 second-order neuron; the somatosensory cortex makes a projection error and attributes the stimulus to the densely innervated face, so pain is felt fronto-orbitally. Only the ophthalmic branch reaches the pars caudalis at C1/C2 (maxillary and mandibular branches end in the pars interpolaris and pars oralis), which is why the cheek and jaw are spared. Innervation is unilateral, so right-sided neck structures refer to the right side of the head.
positive: In referred pain, pressure on the painful (referred) region does not increase pain, whereas pressure on the sensitised source increases pain in the referred area.

accuracy.source: n/a (explanation page; reference Johnston et al. 2013)

notes: Not a test. ⚠ The page body heading reads 'Somatic & Visceral Referred Pain Explained | Pain Neurophysiology' (copied from the referred-pain post it recommends reading first). Reference list printed twice.

title: Watson Headache Test
purpose: Manual provocation of the upper cervical segments (C0-C1 and C2-3) to reproduce head pain in tension-type headache and migraine without aura.
structure: Atlanto-occipital joint (technique 1) and C2-3 segment (technique 2); convergence of cervical afferents onto trigeminal nuclei referring pain temporofrontally.
procedure: Technique 1: patient supine, head rotated 20 degrees away from the headache side (bilateral headache: away from the side the C2 spinous process deviates towards); thumb pressure over the posterior arch of C1 while the other hand rotates the head ipsilaterally, stressing the atlanto-occipital joint; hold 5 s. Technique 2: head rotated about 30 degrees; thumb pressure over the contralateral articular pillar of C2, stressing C2-3; hold 5 s. Patient answers yes/no to reproduction of head pain.
positive: Reproduction of the patient's head pain.

accuracy.source: none; Watson & Drummond 2012 (Headache): intra-rater reliability kappa 0.667 (symptom response) and 1 (mobility grading); tension-type and migraine patients had more head pain referral than controls

notes: Source: moderate clinical value, no further validation. Reference list printed twice; page heading 'Headache &Dizziness' missing a space.
